citations.quote: Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim: First fix a deterministic complex symmetric matrix $A$. Since $A_{ji}=A_{ij}$, $$\xi^{\mathsf T}A\xi-\operatorname{tr}A =\sum_i A_{ii}(\xi_i^2-1)+2\sum_{i<j}A_{ij}\xi_i\xi_j.$$ The diagonal summands have mean zero. Distinct diagonal summands are uncorrelated; a diagonal summand and an off-diagonal summand are uncorrelated because at least one independent centered coordinate occurs to the first power; and two off-diagonal summands are uncorrelated unless their unordered index pairs coincide. Therefore $$\mathbb E\left|\xi^{\mathsf T}A\xi-\operatorname{tr}A\right|^2 =(\mu_4-1)\sum_i|A_{ii}|^2+4\sum_{i<j}|A_{ij}|^2 \le C_{\mu_4}\sum_{i,j}|A_{ij}|^2.$$ Here $\mu_4\ge1$ follows from $\mathbb E\xi_i^2=1$ and Cauchy–Schwarz.

By [F2], the joint law of $(\xi,A)$ is the product of its marginal laws. The integrand is integrable: $|\xi^{\mathsf T}A\xi-\operatorname{tr}A|^2\le2\|A\|_F^2\|\xi\|_2^4+2d\|A\|_F^2$, and $\mathbb E\|\xi\|_2^4<\infty$ because $d$ is finite and $\mathbb E\xi_i^4<\infty$. Thus [F3] permits integration of the deterministic inequality in step 1.1 against the law of $A$, giving the asserted bound.

derivations.claim: By [F1], write $B=U\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_d)U^{\mathsf T}$ with $\lambda_j\ge0$. Thus $R$ exists, is normal, and $$x^{\mathsf T}Rx=\sum_j\frac{(U^{\mathsf T}x)_j^2}{\lambda_j-z},\qquad \operatorname{Im}(x^{\mathsf T}Rx)=\eta\sum_j\frac{(U^{\mathsf T}x)_j^2}{(\lambda_j-u)^2+\eta^2}.$$ If $x\ne0$, this imaginary part is strictly positive, so $1+x^{\mathsf T}Rx\ne0$; if $x=0$, the denominator is $1$.

For positive integers $n$ and $p$, let $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$ and define its (uncentered, unit-variance-normalized) sample covariance matrix by
$$S(X):=\frac1nX^{\mathsf T}X\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}.$$
It is real symmetric and non-negative. If its eigenvalues, counted with multiplicity, are $\lambda_1(S(X)),\ldots,\lambda_p(S(X))$, its empirical spectral distribution (ESD), normalized by the matrix dimension $p$, is
$$\mu_{S(X)}:=\frac1p\sum_{j=1}^p\delta_{\lambda_j(S(X))}.$$
The largest eigenvalue is $\lambda_{\max}(S(X)):=\max_j\lambda_j(S(X))$. When $S(X)$ has at least one positive eigenvalue, its smallest positive eigenvalue is $\lambda_{\min}^{+}(S(X)):=\min\{\lambda_j(S(X)):\lambda_j(S(X))>0\}$. For a sequence $X_n\in\mathbb R^{n\times p_n}$, write $S_n=S(X_n)$ and $\mu_n=\mu_{S_n}$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space, let $n\ge1$, and let $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in X$. Define

$$P_n(A):=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{x_i}(A),\qquad A\in\mathcal A.$$

Then $P_n$ is a probability measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

derivations.claim: The matrix $S(X)$ is symmetric because $(X^{\mathsf T}X)^{\mathsf T}=X^{\mathsf T}X$. For every $v\in\mathbb R^p$, $$v^{\mathsf T}S(X)v=\frac1n\|Xv\|_2^2\ge0.$$ By [F2], its eigenvalues are real; if $S(X)v=\lambda v$ with $v\ne0$, the displayed quadratic-form identity gives $\lambda\|v\|_2^2\ge0$, hence $\lambda\ge0$.

Apply [F3] to the finite list $\lambda_1(S(X)),\ldots,\lambda_p(S(X))$ in the Borel space $\mathbb R$. The resulting empirical measure is exactly [F1] and is a Borel probability measure. Step 1.1 shows it assigns no mass outside $[0,\infty)$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $B$ be a real symmetric non-negative $d\times d$ matrix, let $x\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $z=u+i\eta$ with $u\in\mathbb R$ and $\eta>0$. Put $R=(B-zI)^{-1}$ and $R_x=(B+xx^{\mathsf T}-zI)^{-1}$. Then $1+x^{\mathsf T}Rx\ne0$,
$$R_x=R-\frac{Rxx^{\mathsf T}R}{1+x^{\mathsf T}Rx},$$
and
$$\left|\operatorname{tr}R_x-\operatorname{tr}R\right|\le\frac1\eta.$$

Assume AC. Let $n\ge1$, let $Z_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be independent random elements, meaning measurable maps ([[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]), with laws $\mu_i$ given by pushforward ([[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]). > Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by

If the tree has $s$ odd-depth (column) vertices, its limiting labeling weight is $\gamma^s$, and its expectation is $v^k$.

For completeness, the tree count can be extracted without any random-matrix theorem. Let $R(z)$ count ordered trees rooted at a row, with an edge contributing $z$ and each column vertex contributing $\gamma$. Let $C(z)$ count column-rooted trees with the same weights, including the root-column weight. The ordered list of subtrees gives, as formal power series, $$R=\frac1{1-zC},\qquad C=\frac\gamma{1-zR}.$$
Writing $H=R-1$, these equations give $C=\gamma+H$ and $$H=z(1+H)(\gamma+H).$$
The formal coefficient identity for $H=z\Phi(H)$ is $$[z^k]H=\frac1k[u^{k-1}]\Phi(u)^k.$$

One direct verification uses formal residues: substitute $z=u/\Phi(u)$ into $\operatorname{Res}H(z)z^{-k-1}dz$. The resulting residue is $\operatorname{Res}(u^{-k}\Phi^k-u^{-k+1}\Phi^{k-1}\Phi')du$; the second coefficient is $(k-1)/k$ times the first, by differentiating $\Phi^k$. This proves the identity, including $k=1$. Applying it gives $$\mu_k(\gamma)=[z^k]H=\sum_{s=1}^k\frac1k\binom{k}{s}\binom{k}{s-1}\gamma^s.$$
Thus $$ET_{n,k}\longrightarrow v^k\mu_k(\gamma).$$ This explicitly counts all leading patterns, and the argument above bounds all nonleading patterns. It does not assume a spectral limit.
For a label assignment $w$, let $M_w$ be its walk monomial and $Z_w=M_w-EM_w$. Expand the fourth centered moment as a sum of $E(Z_{w_1}Z_{w_2}Z_{w_3}Z_{w_4})$, with normalization $n^{-4k-4}$.

Join two of the four walks when their sets of matrix entries share an edge. A walk isolated in this graph is independent of the other three monomials, so its centered factor makes the expectation zero. Therefore every surviving configuration has at most two clusters of walks. Each cluster has a connected union graph because its walks are individually connected and consecutive walks in the cluster share an edge.

Moreover, no matrix-entry edge can occur just once in the total $8k$ factors. Indeed, if that edge occurs in $M_{w_t}$, then $EM_{w_t}=0$, so $Z_{w_t}=M_{w_t}$, and conditioning on all other entries makes the expectation zero. Thus a surviving configuration has at most $4k$ distinct edges. Its number of distinct vertices is at most the sum over its clusters of (edges plus one), hence at most $4k+2$. Sharing vertices between different edge-clusters only reduces this bound.

There are finitely many patterns at this fixed $k$. Bounded entries bound every centered product expectation by a constant depending only on $k$ and the entry bound. With $p_n=O(n)$, the count of labelings is $O(n^{4k+2})$. Therefore $$E|T_{n,k}-ET_{n,k}|^4=O(n^{-2}).$$

Markov's inequality and the first Borel–Cantelli lemma show $T_{n,k}-ET_{n,k}\to0$ almost surely. Intersecting over all integer $k\ge1$ proves simultaneous fixed-degree trace convergence for bounded entries. Neither independence between different $n$ nor a monotone sequence $p_n$ was assumed.
**Rectangular strong law.** For every integrable iid nonnegative array $Z_{ij}$, $$\frac1{n^2}\sum_{i\le n,j\le p_n}Z_{ij}\longrightarrow\gamma EZ\quad\hbox{almost surely}.$$

To prove this, for each positive rational $t$ enumerate the cells of the nested rectangles $[m]\times[\lfloor tm\rfloor]$ in their successive increments. This is an enumeration of the whole quadrant, so the ordinary one-dimensional iid strong law applies at the rectangle cardinalities. It gives the limit $tEZ$ after division by $m^2$. Intersect these probability-one events over rational $t$. Bracket $p_n/n$ between rationals $t_-<\gamma<t_+$ and use nonnegativity, then let $t_\pm\to\gamma$. This proof accommodates arbitrary $p_n/n\to\gamma$.

**Singular-value comparison.** For two real rectangular matrices $A,B$ of the same dimensions, pad their ordered singular-value lists with zeros to length $n$ when forming $AA^T,BB^T$. Then $$\sum_{i=1}^n(s_i(A)-s_i(B))^2\le\|A-B\|_F^2.$$ Here is an elementary proof of the underlying comparison. For symmetric matrices $U,V$ of dimension $d$ with ordered eigenvalues $\alpha,\beta$, orthogonal diagonalization expresses $\operatorname{Tr}(UV)$ as $\sum_{ij}\alpha_i\beta_jd_{ij}$, where $d_{ij}$ is the square of an orthogonal overlap and its row and column sums are one. For descending real sequences, this sum is at most $\sum_i\alpha_i\beta_i$: set $c_i=\sum_jd_{ij}\beta_j$; the sum of its first $r$ entries is at most the sum of the first $r$ entries of $\beta$, because the associated column weights lie in $[0,1]$ and sum to $r$. Summation by parts against descending $\alpha$, with equal total sums, proves the assertion. Expanding $\operatorname{Tr}(U-V)^2$ now bounds it below by $\sum_i(\alpha_i-\beta_i)^2$. Apply this result to the symmetric dilations $$\begin{pmatrix}0&A\\A^T&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \begin{pmatrix}0&B\\B^T&0\end{pmatrix}.$$
Their eigenvalues are the singular values, their negatives, and the required zeros. Both sides acquire a factor two, proving the comparison.

For $k\ge1$, the scalar factorization and Cauchy–Schwarz consequently give $$\left|\frac1n\sum_i s_i^{2k}-\frac1n\sum_i t_i^{2k}\right|\le2k\left(\frac{\|A-B\|_F^2}{n}\right)^{1/2}\left[\frac2n\sum_i(s_i^{4k-2}+t_i^{4k-2})\right]^{1/2}.$$ Indeed $|s^{2k}-t^{2k}|\le2k|s-t|(s^{2k-1}+t^{2k-1})$ for nonnegative $s,t$; squaring the last parenthesis is bounded by twice the sum of the squares. This inequality needs no operator-norm bound on $B$.
For integer $K\ge1$, put $$m_K=E[\xi\mathbf1_{|\xi|\le K}],\qquad \eta^{(K)}=\xi\mathbf1_{|\xi|\le K}-m_K,\qquad v_K=E(\eta^{(K)})^2.$$
Then $0\le v_K\le1$ and $v_K\to1$. The residual $r_K=\xi-\eta^{(K)}$ has second moment $$\delta_K^2=Er_K^2=E[\xi^2\mathbf1_{|\xi|>K}]-m_K^2\longrightarrow0.$$

Let $B_n^{(K)}$ be the normalized matrix of these bounded centered entries, constructed from the same original array. On one probability-one event, phases 1–2 give for every integer $K$ and every integer $j\ge1$ $$\frac1n\operatorname{Tr}(B_n^{(K)}B_n^{(K)T})^j\longrightarrow v_K^j\mu_j(\gamma).$$
The rectangular strong law, applied to $r_K^2$, also gives simultaneously in $K$ $$\frac1n\|A_n-B_n^{(K)}\|_F^2\longrightarrow\gamma\delta_K^2.$$

Intersect this event with the original coarse-norm event. For each outcome in the intersection there is a finite $C$ such that $\|A_n\|\le C$ eventually. Thus the $s_i^{4k-2}$ average in the comparison inequality is at most $C^{4k-2}$. The $t_i^{4k-2}$ average converges to $v_K^{2k-1}\mu_{2k-1}(\gamma)\le\mu_{2k-1}(\gamma)$. Consequently $$\limsup_n\left|\frac1n\operatorname{Tr}S_n^k-v_K^k\mu_k(\gamma)\right|\le2k\sqrt{\gamma}\,\delta_K\sqrt{2(C^{4k-2}+\mu_{2k-1}(\gamma))}.$$
Let $K\to\infty$. This proves, simultaneously for every fixed positive integer $k$, $$\frac1n\operatorname{Tr}S_n^k\longrightarrow\mu_k(\gamma)\quad\hbox{almost surely}.$$

In particular $n^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}S_n\to\gamma>0$, so eventually there is at least one positive eigenvalue. Every fixed polynomial with zero constant term has its normalized trace limit by linearity. There is no triangular truncation, hidden high-moment assumption, or appeal to an empirical-distribution limit.
Set $c=1+\gamma$, $d=2\sqrt\gamma$, so $a=c-d$, $b=c+d$, and define on $(a,b)$ $$w(x)=\frac1{2\pi}\sqrt{(b-x)(x-a)}.$$

We prove the exact positive-moment identity $$\mu_k(\gamma)=\int_a^b x^{k-1}w(x)\,dx\qquad(k\ge1).$$ This is only an identity for explicit numbers and integrals. No probability measure or spectral support theorem is asserted or used.

For real $z>0$ sufficiently small, substitute $x=c+d\cos\theta$. The generating function of the right-hand side is $$z\int_a^b\frac{w(x)}{1-zx}\,dx=\frac{zd^2}{2\pi}\int_0^\pi\frac{\sin^2\theta}{1-cz-dz\cos\theta}\,d\theta.$$

For $u>|v|$, substitution $t=\tan(\theta/2)$ directly gives $\int_0^\pi(u-v\cos\theta)^{-1}d\theta=\pi/\sqrt{u^2-v^2}$. Polynomial division in $\cos\theta$ then gives $$\int_0^\pi\frac{\sin^2\theta}{u-v\cos\theta}\,d\theta=\frac\pi{v^2}\left(u-\sqrt{u^2-v^2}\right),$$ with its continuous value when $v=0$. Hence the generating function above equals $$\frac{1-cz-\sqrt{(1-cz)^2-4\gamma z^2}}{2z}.$$

It is analytic near zero, vanishes there, and solves $H=z(1+H)(\gamma+H)$. The formal equation uniquely determines the coefficients recursively, so these coefficients equal the tree counts of phase 1. Expansion under the integral is justified by the uniformly convergent geometric series on $[a,b]$ for small $z$. This proves the identity, also when $a=0$.
Consequently, for every polynomial $P$ with $P(0)=0$, $$\frac1n\operatorname{Tr}P(S_n)\longrightarrow\int_a^b\frac{P(x)}x w(x)\,dx.$$
At $a=0$, the quotient is the polynomial obtained by canceling the factor $x$, so there is no singularity to interpret.
Fix $L$ with $0<L<b$. For an integer $q\ge0$ use $P_q(x)=x^{q+1}(x-L)$. Its trace limit is $$I_q=\int_a^b x^q(x-L)w(x)\,dx.$$

Choose $\max(a,L)<t<u<b$. The positive contribution from $[t,u]$ is at least $t^q(t-L)\int_t^u w(x)dx$. The absolute negative contribution, supported in $[a,L]$ when that interval is nonempty, is at most $L^q L\int_a^b w(x)dx$. Since $t>L$ and $w>0$ on $(a,b)$, $I_q>0$ for some finite integer $q$ (and for all sufficiently large $q$). If $L\le a$, positivity follows directly.

If all eigenvalues of $S_n$ were at most $L$, every summand $P_q(\lambda)$ would be nonpositive, contradicting the eventually positive normalized trace. Thus $\lambda_{\max}(S_n)>L$ for all sufficiently large $n$. Intersecting over a countable sequence $L\uparrow b$ gives $\liminf\lambda_{\max}\ge b$.

Fix $U>a$. If desired replace $U$ by a smaller number in $(a,b)$; proving the stronger bound for that smaller threshold proves the original bound. Thus assume $a<U<b$. Choose a fixed $B>b$ and use the polynomial $$Q_q(x)=x(U-x)(B-x)^{2q},\qquad q\ge0.$$

For every $x\ge0$, it vanishes at $0$, is nonpositive for $x\ge U$, and is positive for $0<x<U$ except at the irrelevant zero of the even factor. Its trace limit is $$J_q=\int_a^b(U-x)(B-x)^{2q}w(x)\,dx.$$
Choose $a<t<u<U$. The positive contribution on $[t,u]$ is at least $$(U-u)(B-u)^{2q}\int_t^u w(x)dx.$$
The absolute negative contribution on $[U,b]$ is at most $$(b-U)(B-U)^{2q}\int_a^b w(x)dx.$$

Because $B-u>B-U>0$ and the positive interval has positive integral, $J_q>0$ for some finite integer $q$. If $S_n$ had no positive eigenvalue below $U$, all its eigenvalues would be either $0$ or at least $U$, and therefore $\operatorname{Tr}Q_q(S_n)\le0$. The positive limiting trace excludes this for every sufficiently large $n$. Hence $\lambda_{\min}^{+}(S_n)<U$ eventually. Let $U\downarrow a$ through a countable sequence to obtain $\limsup\lambda_{\min}^{+}\le a$.

For $\gamma=1$, $a=0$. The same argument chooses $0<t<u<U$ and proves an eventually positive eigenvalue below every prescribed $U>0$. The factor $x$ removes every exact zero eigenvalue, including arbitrary extra rank defects, so no rank theorem or lower-rank estimate is concealed in this case. Since eigenvalues are nonnegative, this also proves $\lambda_{\min}^{+}\to0$ in the square-aspect-ratio case.

Let $(\xi_{ij})_{i,j\ge1}$ be one infinite iid real array with $E\xi_{11}=0$, $E\xi_{11}^2=1$ and $E|\xi_{11}|^4<\infty$. Consider any deterministic rectangular sequence $R_n\times C_n$ with both $R_n/n$ and $C_n/n$ bounded above and bounded away from zero. Write $X_n=(\xi_{ij})_{i\le R_n,j\le C_n}$ and $N_n=\max(R_n,C_n)$. There is a deterministic sequence $\delta_n\to0$, which may be chosen to decrease more slowly than any specified finite list of rates tending to zero and to satisfy $\delta_n\ge1/\log(n+2)$, such that, almost surely, $X_n$ equals its entrywise truncation at $\delta_n\sqrt{N_n}$ eventually. Set
$$\widehat\xi_{ij}^{(n)}=\xi_{ij}\mathbf1_{\{|\xi_{ij}|\le\delta_n\sqrt{N_n}\}},\quad\mu_n=E\widehat\xi_{11}^{(n)},\quad x_{ij}^{(n)}=\widehat\xi_{ij}^{(n)}-\mu_n.$$
Then $\sqrt{R_nC_n/N_n}|\mu_n|\to0$, $E|x_{11}^{(n)}|^2\le1$ tends to $1$, $|x_{ij}^{(n)}|\le2\delta_n\sqrt{N_n}$ eventually, and $E|x_{11}^{(n)}|^q\le K(2\delta_n\sqrt{N_n})^{q-3}$ for every integer $q\ge3$, with $K$ independent of $n,q$. Almost surely the following controls hold for the original entries and for the centered truncated entries:
$$\max_{i\le R_n}\left|N_n^{-1}\sum_{j\le C_n}|x_{ij}^{(n)}|^2-C_n/N_n\right|\to0,\qquad\max_{j\le C_n}\left|N_n^{-1}\sum_{i\le R_n}|x_{ij}^{(n)}|^2-R_n/N_n\right|\to0,$$
$$\max_{i\le R_n,j\le C_n}|x_{ij}^{(n)}|/\sqrt{N_n}\to0,\qquad N_n^{-2}\sum_{i\le R_n,j\le C_n}|x_{ij}^{(n)}|^4=O(1).$$
For every fixed $q>2$, the rectangular matrix with entry $N_n^{-q/2}|x_{ij}^{(n)}|^q$ has Frobenius norm tending to zero; the assertion also holds with a sign attached to each entry.

Let $(\xi_{ij})_{i,j\ge1}$ be one infinite real iid array with $E\xi_{11}=0$, $E\xi_{11}^2=1$ and $E|\xi_{11}|^4<\infty$, and let $p_h/h\to\gamma\in(0,\infty)$. Put $N_h=\max(h,p_h)$, $m_h=\min(h,p_h)$ and $y_h=m_h/N_h\to y:=\min(\gamma,\gamma^{-1})$. Take the centered slow truncations of the upper-left $h\times p_h$ blocks, orient each with $m_h$ rows and $N_h$ columns, and divide by $\sqrt{N_h}$, obtaining $Y_h$. For each fixed integer $\ell\ge1$, define $T_{h,\ell}$ by summing the products of the entries of $Y_h,Y_h^{\mathsf T},\ldots,Y_h,Y_h^{\mathsf T}$ along all paths of length $2\ell$, subject to every pair of vertices two positions apart being unequal. Its row and column endpoints are included in these exclusions. Then almost surely
$$\limsup_h\|T_{h,\ell}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le(2\ell+1)(\ell+1)y^{(\ell-1)/2}.$$
In particular, for the original untruncated $X_h=(\xi_{ij})_{i\le h,j\le p_h}$, almost surely $\limsup_h\|X_h/\sqrt h\|_{\mathrm{op}}<\infty$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

In the rest of the proof write $n=N_h$, $p=m_h$, $y_h=p/n\to y\in(0,1]$, and $Y$ for this centered normalized matrix. F2 gives every fixed-length bound for $T_j$, in particular $\|Y\|=O(1)$. The diagonal laws give $D=\operatorname{diag}(YY^{\mathsf T})\to I$ and $E=\operatorname{diag}(Y^{\mathsf T}Y)\to yI$ in operator norm. Set $T=T_1$ and $T_0=I$. All limits below are along the original sequence index $h$.

For compatible alternating rectangular matrices, write $A_1\odot\cdots\odot A_s$ for the path sum imposing $i_r\ne i_{r+2}$ at every available position (including endpoints). Its norm is at most $2^{s-1}\prod\|A_i\|$. Here is a local proof rather than an appeal to Appendix A. Expand at the first forbidden reversal: $$A_1\odot\cdots\odot A_s=A_1(A_2\odot\cdots\odot A_s)-\operatorname{diag}(A_1A_2)(A_3\odot\cdots\odot A_s)+(A_1\circ A_2^{\mathsf T}\circ A_3)\odot A_4\odot\cdots\odot A_s.$$

The correction restores the additional exclusion lost when the first reversal is contracted. This identity follows by fixing the indices $i_1=i_3$, then excluding $i_2=i_4$; for $s=2$ it is simply deletion of the diagonal. Rectangular diagonal matrices have the compatible rectangular identity embedding where necessary. The diagonal term has norm at most $\|A_1\|\|A_2\|$. The fused Schur product has norm at most $\|A_1\|\|A_2\|\|A_3\|$: it is a compression of $A_1\otimes A_2^{\mathsf T}\otimes A_3$ by the coordinate isometries $e_a\mapsto e_a\otimes e_a\otimes e_a$ and the analogous column isometry. The tensor-product norm bound follows by factoring a tensor operator into maps acting on one coordinate at a time; each such map is an orthogonal direct sum of copies of that factor and therefore has norm at most its norm, by summing the squared block norms. With $c_1=1$, $c_2=2$, induction gives $c_s\le c_{s-1}+2c_{s-2}\le2^{s-1}$.

Define $Y^{[q]}$ to have entries $n^{-q/2}|x|^{q-1}x$ for odd $q$ and $n^{-q/2}|x|^q$ for even $q$. The strong-law inputs give $\|Y^{[2]}\|_F^2=O(1)$ and $\|Y^{[q]}\|_F^2\le(\max|x|/\sqrt n)^{2q-4}n^{-2}\sum|x|^4\to0$ for $q>2$. By F2, $\|Y\|^2\le\|T\|+\|\operatorname{diag}(YY^*)\|=O(1)$. Thus every fixed-length restricted product with at least one factor $Y^{[q]}$, $q>2$, is $o(1)$ in norm.

Centering comparison is now legitimate without circularity: F2 proves the graph estimate for centered truncations and bounds their $\|Y\|=O(1)$ using their row law; the mean matrix has norm $\sqrt p\,|E x_{11}^{\mathrm{tr}}|=o(1)$ by F1. Expand the difference of fixed-length restricted products multilinearly and apply the norm inequality. There are $2^{2j}-1$ terms, not the book's printed $2j-1$.

Let $D=\operatorname{diag}(YY^*)\to I$, $E=\operatorname{diag}(Y^*Y)\to yI$ in norm. Let $B_j$ be the restricted product of length $2j-1$ starting with $Y^*$ and alternating thereafter. For $j\ge2$, the deterministic restricted-product identity above gives $$T_j=YB_j-DT_{j-1}+Y^{[3]}\odot Y^*\odot\cdots\odot Y^*=YB_j-T_{j-1}+o(1).$$
For $j=1$, $YB_1=T_1+D=T_1+T_0+o(1)$, so the unified relation is $YB_j=T_j+T_{j-1}+o(1)$ for all $j\ge1$. Similarly $$B_{j+1}=Y^*T_j-EB_j+(Y^{[3]})^*\odot Y\odot\cdots\odot Y^*.$$

For $j=1$ the final correction is simply $(Y^{[3]})^*$, which is $o(1)$; this case must not be silently omitted. All restricted products have fixed length and bounded norm; the fused corrections vanish by the estimates above. Therefore $$T_{j+1}=YB_{j+1}-DT_j+o(1)=(YY^*-D)T_j-yYB_j+o(1)=TT_j-yT_j-yT_{j-1}+o(1).$$
Errors are in operator norm, for each fixed $j$. The recurrence holds with $T_0=I$ and includes $j=1$.

Put $H=T-yI$. Define $P_0(z)=1$, $P_1(z)=z+y$, and $P_{j+1}(z)=zP_j(z)-yP_{j-1}(z)$. Since $\|H\|=O(1)$, induction in the recurrence gives $T_j=P_j(H)+o(1)$ for each fixed $j$. Explicitly $$P_j(z)=y^{j/2}\left[U_j\left(\frac z{2\sqrt y}\right)+\sqrt y\,U_{j-1}\left(\frac z{2\sqrt y}\right)\right],$$ where $U_{-1}=0$, $U_0=1$, $U_{j+1}(t)=2tU_j(t)-U_{j-1}(t)$. This explicit formula follows immediately by checking the two initial values and recurrence.

For real $|t|\ge1+\epsilon$, write $|t|=\cosh a$ and $\rho=e^a>1$. The recurrence directly gives $U_j(\cosh a)=\sinh((j+1)a)/\sinh a$ and $U_j(-t)=(-1)^jU_j(t)$. Hence $|U_j(t)|\ge\rho^j$ and $|U_{j-1}(t)|/|U_j(t)|\le\rho^{-1}$, the last inequality following from $\sinh(ja)/\sinh((j+1)a)<e^{-a}$. Therefore $|U_j(t)+\sqrt yU_{j-1}(t)|\ge(1-\sqrt y/\rho)\rho^j\ge(1-\rho^{-1})\rho^j$. This is strictly positive uniformly for $|t|\ge1+\epsilon$, including $y=1$. If $\|H\|>2\sqrt y+\epsilon$ infinitely often, the finite-dimensional spectral theorem and spectral mapping for a polynomial give, for every fixed $j$, $y^{j/2}(1-\rho_\epsilon^{-1})\rho_\epsilon^j\le\limsup\|P_j(H)\|\le(2j+1)(j+1)y^{(j-1)/2}$ with a fixed $\rho_\epsilon>1$.

The inequality in step 11.1 is impossible for all positive integers $j$: after dividing by $y^{j/2}$, its left side grows exponentially in $j$ while the right side is the polynomial $(2j+1)(j+1)y^{-1/2}$. Thus almost surely $\limsup_h\|H\|\le2\sqrt y$. Since $YY^{\mathsf T}-(1+y)I-H=D-I\to0$, the centered matrices satisfy the stated confinement. All fixed-$j$ estimates hold simultaneously by intersecting countably many probability-one events.

Let $A_h$ denote the original oriented upper-left block divided by $\sqrt{N_h}$. F1 gives $\|A_h-Y_h\|\to0$ through eventual truncation equality and the explicit constant-mean norm, while F2 gives $\|Y_h\|=O(1)$ and hence $\|A_h\|=O(1)$. Since the argument allowed $y_h=1$ and orientation changes, it includes the square-aspect boundary.
